items.prompt:
Invented weekly schedules for the fictional Khomas Bean Stall in Windhoek. Price in N$ per bag: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Original quantity demanded in bags: 100, 80, 60, 40, 20. Quantity supplied: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100. New quantity demanded: 140, 120, 100, 80, 60. Supply conditions remain unchanged.

Explain the effect of the stated increase in demand using a diagram constructed from the supplied schedules. Label both equilibria and distinguish a demand shift from movement along a curve.
items.canonical_answer: Price goes vertically in N$ per bag and quantity horizontally in bags per week. Plot D, S and D1 from the schedules. D and S meet at N$30/60 bags; D1 and S meet at N$40/80 bags. Demand has shifted right while supply has not shifted. Buyers want more at each price, so equilibrium moves up the supply curve to a higher price and quantity.
marking_guidance: Axes/labels (1): correct price and quantity axes with units. Original curves (2): accurately plot original demand (1) and supply (1). Original equilibrium (1): N$30 and 60 bags. Change/control (1): rightward D1 with S fixed. New equilibrium (1): N$40 and 80 bags. Explanation/interpretation (1): increased demand moves equilibrium up the unchanged supply curve. Total 7.

Analyse the change in the equilibrium and explain why it is not caused solely by a change in the product’s own price.
items.canonical_answer: Equilibrium price rises from N$30 to N$40 and quantity from 60 to 80 bags. New demand is 40 bags higher at every listed price, so it is a shift rather than movement along the original curve. The increased price induces more supply along the unchanged supply curve.
marking_guidance: Relationship/pattern (1): both equilibrium price and quantity increase. Evidence/comparison (1): N$30/60 to N$40/80. Explanation/reason (2): demand rises at each price (1), distinguishing a shift from an own-price movement (1). Total 4.
